title: LIBYA: Political prisoners in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli (UA 188/96)
summary: Urgent action about political prisoners in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli, after a reported mutiny said to have begun around 5 July 1996 and lasted about a week. Amnesty reports that prisoners complained of poor medical care, hygiene, overcrowding and food, and held guards hostage. Special security forces reportedly stormed the prison and fired on prisoners and hostages, killing scores. Amnesty had written to Gaddafi asking for an impartial inquiry and had no reply. It asked for the names of the dead to be published and for access to doctors, lawyers and families.

title: LIBYA: Amnesty International calls for an independent investigation and urges against the use of the death penalty
summary: Amnesty news release urging Gaddafi to order a prompt, impartial inquiry into the killings of many political prisoners at Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli, in early July 1996, and to publish the names of the dead. It repeats reports of a week-long mutiny over medical care, sanitation, overcrowding and food, followed by a storming by special security forces. It also reports that on 16 July 1996 Libyan television announced new capital offences (profiteering in wartime or blockade, drug, alcohol and currency offences), published in the gazette on 15 July. Note the date discrepancy with Human Rights Watch, which places the Abu Salim killings on 28-30 June 1996.

title: Libya: Further information on political detention
collection: AI Index MDE 19/03/92 (date inferred from content; not printed on the page)
summary: Amnesty says it knows of at least 554 political prisoners in Libya, including 127 names not previously published, and details 30 cases. At least 14 of the 15 prisoners in Appendix I are believed held at Abu Salim detention centre on the outskirts of Tripoli, as are most people arrested after the May 1984 Bab al-Aziziya attack claimed by the NFSL. Cases include Tripoli university staff and students, and a Tripoli Postal Service employee. It reports torture methods (falaqa, electric shocks, mock executions) and says Abu Salim prisoners before 1986 lacked proper medical care. It notes the March 1988 release of 400 prisoners while about 100 were excluded.

title: LIBYA: Amnesty International completes first fact-finding visit in over five years
summary: Amnesty reports on a 15-23 May 2009 visit invited by the Gaddafi Foundation. Delegates visited prisoners at Jdeida (run by the General People's Committee of Justice), and at Ain Zara and Abu Salim prisons (apparently under Public Security), but were refused access to other prisoners and to relatives of the disappeared in Benghazi. It raises the Internal Security Agency's incommunicado detention and the State Security Court created in 2007. It notes the reported 10 May 2009 suicide of Ibn al-Shaykh al-Libi at Abu Salim, with no autopsy access, and the death in Amman of Fathi el-Jahmi, who had been held at Tripoli Medical Centre.

title: Libya: 30 years on - time for action
summary: Marking 30 years of Gaddafi rule, Amnesty says hundreds of political prisoners are held without charge or trial, some for over a decade, and that torture, deaths in custody and disappearances continue. It names al-Wafi Nbiyya (sentenced after the 1993 Misrata army rebellion) and Mohammad Ali Bakoush (held without trial since February 1989) as having died in Abu Salim prison, Tripoli, in July or August 1999. It also says five prisoners of conscience convicted in 1973 over the Islamic Liberation Party were reportedly still serving life terms there. It criticises the 1997 Charter of Honour, which allows collective punishment. Embargoed until 31 August 1999.

title: Libya: Amnesty International's prisoner concerns in the light of recent legal reforms
summary: Amnesty states that despite the March 1988 amnesty and subsequent legal reforms, at least 467 political prisoners remained detained, some possibly prisoners of conscience. It singles out continuing arbitrary arrest and incommunicado detention and names five cases. Appendices list detainees and outline the legislation used to restrict expression. The catalogue page does not give Tripoli place details; the full PDF should be consulted.

title: LIBYA: Six men, names not known to Amnesty International (UA 352/92)
summary: Urgent action after Libyan television announced on 10 November 1992 that six men convicted of offences including rape and murder were executed that morning. Amnesty calls these the first officially announced executions in over five years; the previous announced ones were nine people convicted of politically motivated crimes in February 1987. It outlines the review chain through the Court of Cassation and the General People's Congress secretariat, and recalls Gaddafi's March 1988 call for abolition. Appeals were addressed to officials in Tripoli.

title: Amnesty International Newsletter, May 1977 (Libya: first executions in 23 years)
summary: Monthly newsletter whose Libya item reports that army officers were executed by firing squad on 2 April 1977, that of 75 tried in December 1976 23 were sentenced to death and the figure rose to 45 on appeal, and that five people were publicly hanged in Benghazi on 7 April. Amnesty cabled Gaddafi on 12 April. The Libya items place the hangings in Benghazi, not Tripoli; the entry is kept as 1977 context. The issue also covers many other countries.

title: Libya: Serious human rights violations amid secrecy and isolation (report: Gross human rights violations amid secrecy and isolation)
summary: Release accompanying a 36-page report saying Libya practices arbitrary arrest, torture, extrajudicial killing and enforced disappearance with impunity. It describes the March 1997 Charter of Honour allowing collective punishment, and hostage-taking of relatives. Rashid 'Abd al-Hamid al-'Urfia, arrested February 1982, is reported still held without charge in Abu Salim Prison, Tripoli; torture is said to occur in underground rooms of Abu Salim, including electric shocks and 'car torture'. Mansur Kikhiya disappeared from Cairo in December 1993.

title: Libya: Evidence Suggests Khamis Brigade Killed 45 Detainees
summary: HRW reports that the Khamis Brigade (32nd Brigade) appears to have shot and grenaded detainees on 23 August 2011 in a warehouse in Khalida Ferjan, Salahaddin, south of Tripoli beside the Yarmouk military base; it was burned three days later. On 27 August HRW counted about 45 bodies in the ashes. A survivor said 153 names were read at roll call, about 20 escaped, and roughly 125 detainees were civilians. A former detainee described 60-80 held at once with one litre of water a day. HRW says murder of detainees is a war crime.

title: Libya: Gaddafi Forces Suspected of Executing Detainees
summary: HRW says forces loyal to Gaddafi probably killed at least 17 detainees around 21 August 2011 in the Al-Amal al-Akhdar building of the Internal Security service, near Gargur, Tripoli, with 17 bodies taken to Matiga hospital on 24 August. On 26 August it inspected 18 bodies in a dry riverbed between Gargur and Bab al-Aziziya and 29 more at a field clinic outside Bab al-Aziziya. It also describes checkpoint killings. HRW had not yet identified those responsible and no forensic analysis was complete.

title: Libya: Words to Deeds - The Urgent Need for Human Rights Reform
summary: 84-page report based on HRW's first Libya visit in April-May 2005, with access to five prisons and 32 prisoners interviewed privately; 15 said they were tortured. It notes Law 71 (1972) banning group activity, the abolition of the People's Court in January 2005, 12,860 prisoners in 34 facilities in April 2005, and that all 131 prisoners a committee recommended releasing were still held on 10 January 2006. Tripoli sites: Abu Salim (June 1996 deaths, October 2005 protest by 135 People's Court prisoners), Jdeida (about 180 death-row prisoners reported), the Police Academy (Brotherhood retrial) and Mitiga airport (former Wheelus Air Base).

title: Libya: June 1996 Killings at Abu Salim Prison
summary: HRW compiles witness accounts of the killing of prisoners at Abu Salim prison, Tripoli, on 28-30 June 1996. Libyan groups abroad put deaths up to about 1,200 of 1,600-1,700 held. It reports that security forces fired and threw grenades on 29 June and that bodies were reportedly buried in trenches. Since 2001 authorities reportedly told 112 families of deaths; 238 families said they had lost contact. Gaddafi acknowledged killings in April 2004. HRW stresses it could not independently verify the accounts.
